unit.unitOverview: Research is finding out about something in a careful, organised way, from several sources, so that you can trust what you learn, weigh different perspectives, and explain it to someone else. It is not just typing a question into a search engine. Real research means asking a focused question that can be debated, gathering information from a range of sources, judging and cross-checking them, recording the important parts in your own words, synthesising them into your own findings, and saying where everything came from.

explainers.title: Welcome back to Global Perspectives
explainers.body:
Hello, and welcome to Unit 1 of Global Perspectives at Ehel Academy. Whether this subject is new to you or you met it last year, one thing stays the same: Global Perspectives is not about memorising facts for a test. It teaches you a set of thinking skills you can carry into any subject, any job, and any decision you will ever make.

There are six skills in Global Perspectives, and you keep growing all of them, year after year:

This unit is about the first of those skills: Research. In Stage 8 you go further than before. You will ask questions that can be argued from more than one perspective, design and test your own questionnaire, cross-check sources against each other, and pull together, or synthesise, what you learn from several sources at once. These are the moves a real researcher makes.

Why does any of this matter beyond school? Think about the decisions adults weigh every week. A journalist checks a story against three sources before printing it. A nurse compares two treatments before advising a patient. A town council studies traffic counts and residents' views before changing a bus route. Every one of them is doing research: asking a sharp question, gathering evidence, judging who to trust, and deciding. The learner who practises these moves now will decide better for the rest of their life. That is why we begin here.
bullets: Research — finding things out about the world in a careful, organised way.
Analysis — taking a topic apart to see its causes, effects and connections.
Evaluation — judging how strong an argument or a piece of evidence really is.
Reflection — thinking honestly about how you learn and how your views change.
Collaboration — working well with other people towards a shared goal.
Communication — sharing your ideas so clearly that others truly understand.

explainers.title: How you will learn this unit
explainers.body:
You are learning the Ehel Academy way, which is self-paced. That means three kinds of support work together, and in Stage 8 you take a little more of the lead yourself:

Older versions of this subject told learners to 'talk to a partner' or 'discuss with the class'. In our model, your AI tutor is your partner and your class. So every 'Ask Your AI Tutor' box is a real conversation. Say or type your ideas, ask it to push back, and let it stretch your thinking further than working alone ever could.
bullets: You, learning at your own pace. You read, think and complete each activity in your own time. Slow down where an idea is hard; move quickly where it is easy. You decide the order and the speed.

Your AI tutor, available every hour of the day. Wherever this book says 'Ask Your AI Tutor', you talk to your tutor as if it were a thoughtful study partner and a whole class rolled into one. It discusses your ideas, questions your thinking, and gives feedback whenever you are ready, day or night.
Your teacher, about twice a week. In live sessions you bring your best work and your sharpest questions, hear other learners' views, and get guidance on where to go next.

explainers.title: Meet Sana, our researcher for this unit
explainers.body:
To make every skill concrete, we will follow one Year 8 learner through the whole unit. Her name is Sana, and she studies at Ehel Academy in Mogadishu.

Sana's neighbourhood is growing fast. Each year there seem to be more cars, more minibuses and more three-wheel taxis on the roads near her home. In the mornings the air by the junction smells of exhaust, and her younger brother, who has a weak chest, coughs more than he used to. Sana starts to wonder: as the traffic grows, what is it doing to the air her family breathes, and what would help the most?

That question becomes Sana's research project for this unit. Each time you meet a new skill, you will see exactly how Sana uses it, from her first rough question to real findings she can share. You will do the very same thing with a topic that matters to you.

explainers.title: Your Challenge: the project that runs through the unit
explainers.body:
This unit builds towards one ongoing project we call your Challenge. A Challenge is a global issue that also matters right where you live. You keep returning to it, lesson after lesson, and each new skill adds another piece. In Stage 8 your Challenge should be one you can look at from several perspectives, not just your own.

Here are some issues that are global and also very real across the Horn of Africa. Any of these could become your Challenge:

You do not have to choose yet. As you work through the skills, keep a note of any issue that makes you curious, or a little bit angry. Strong curiosity and a quiet 'someone should fix this' are excellent signs of a good Challenge. The best Stage 8 topics are ones where thoughtful people genuinely disagree, because that gives you something to research and argue.
bullets: Clean air and the growth of traffic in our towns
Growing towns and what happens to open spaces and wildlife (urbanisation)
How people get around, and whether public transport works for everyone
Work and training for young people leaving school
Plastic waste on our streets and along the Berbera coast
Renewable energy, such as solar power for homes and schools
Healthy food and good school meals
Road safety on busy roads
Clean water and safe sanitation for every family
Why people move from the countryside into cities (migration)

explainers.title: What is research, really?
explainers.body:
Plenty of people think research just means typing a question online and reading the first result. Real research is far more careful. Research is finding out about something in an organised way, from several sources, so that you can trust what you learn, weigh different views, and explain it clearly to others.

Good research moves through a cycle. At Stage 8 the cycle has a few extra, more demanding steps:

Notice that 'search online' is only a small part of one step. Strong researchers also talk to people, design surveys, watch what really happens, and read printed material. And they never trust a single source on its own.
bullets: Ask a clear question worth arguing, and break it into sub-questions.
Predict what you expect to find, and choose methods to test it.
Gather information from several primary and secondary sources.
Judge each source, and cross-check it against the others.
Record the important parts in your own words.
Bring the sources together, or synthesise them, into your own findings.
Present your findings clearly, and reference every source you used.

explainers.title: Keep a research log
explainers.body:
Before you meet the first skill, start a habit every real researcher relies on: keep a research log. This is a notebook or a document where you record everything about your Challenge as you go. Each time you work, write the date and note what you did, what you found, which source it came from, and how much you trust it.

A research log earns its place for three reasons. It keeps your sources and notes together so nothing is lost, and so you can always reference a fact later. It shows how your thinking changes over time, which you will need for Reflection. And it makes writing up your findings far easier, because the work is already there, source by source. Keep your log beside you as you read on.

explainers.title: Skill 1 (1.1): Asking a research question you can argue
explainers.body:
Every strong project begins with a strong question. A weak question wastes your time, because you can never really answer it. A good Stage 8 research question has four features. It is interesting, it is clear, it is focused, and above all it can be argued.

That last feature is what lifts a Stage 8 question above a Stage 7 one. A question that can be argued lets you develop, and even change, your own point of view on an issue, and back it with evidence you have gathered. If a question has only one correct answer, there is nothing to argue and little to research.
bullets: Interesting means it matters to you and to other people, so the research is worth doing.
Clear means anyone could read it and know exactly what you are asking.
Focused means it is not too broad, not too narrow and not too vague. Too broad and you can never finish; too narrow and there is nothing to find out; too vague and you cannot tell what to research.
Can be argued means people could reasonably answer it in different ways. You have to weigh evidence and form a perspective, rather than look up one plain fact.

explainers.title: Skill 2 (1.1): Breaking your question into sub-questions
explainers.body: A good research question is usually too big to answer in one go. The trick is to break it into smaller sub-questions. Each sub-question is easier to research on its own, and together they add up to an answer for the big one. Writing sub-questions is a skill Cambridge expects you to build in Stage 8.

explainers.title: Skill 3 (1.2): Knowing your sources - primary, secondary, print and multimedia
explainers.body:
Information comes from sources. A source is anywhere your information comes from: a book, a website, a video, a person, or something you see for yourself. Sources come in two main types.

Strong research uses both. Secondary sources give you the bigger picture and facts others have already found. Primary sources tell you what is true right here, in your own community, which no book could know. At Stage 8 you are expected to move confidently between the two, and to draw on a range rather than leaning on just one.
bullets: Primary sources give first-hand information that you gather yourself. Interviews you carry out, questionnaires you run, and things you observe are all primary sources.
Secondary sources are made by someone else who studied the issue before you. Books, news articles, websites and reports are secondary sources.

explainers.title: Skill 4 (1.3): Making a prediction and choosing a method to test it
explainers.body:
Before gathering first-hand information, good researchers make a prediction. A prediction is a clear statement of what you think will happen, or what you think is causing something. For example: 'Increased traffic will increase air pollution,' or 'People living far from a clinic get less healthcare.' Then you choose a method to test whether your prediction holds. The main methods are:

You choose the method that fits your question. Want numbers from many people? Use a questionnaire. Want the full story from one person? Use an interview. Want to know what really happens? Use observation. Want the wider picture first? Start with secondary research.
bullets: Questionnaire or survey — the same set of questions given to many people, to find out what a lot of people think or do.
Interview — a deeper conversation with one person or a small group, to understand their views in detail.
Observation — carefully watching and recording what actually happens.
Secondary research — using an internet search, reports or articles to find what others have already discovered.

explainers.title: Skill 5 (1.3): Designing and testing a good questionnaire
explainers.body:
A questionnaire is one of the most powerful primary methods, but only if the questions are well made. In Stage 8 you design your own, test it on real people, and improve it. A good question to gather information should:

A leading or biased question tips people towards a particular reply. For example, 'Why don't more people leave their cars at home and use the bus?' already assumes buses are better, so it is biased. A fair version would be, 'How do you usually travel, and why?' Aim for a balance too: some questions can be answered with a simple yes or no, while others invite more detail.
bullets: Use words with clear meanings, so everyone reads it the same way.
Be short and easy to understand.
Be able to be answered quickly.
Not offer too many options to choose from.
Not be leading, and not contain bias that pushes people toward one answer.

explainers.title: Skill 6 (1.2): Judging a source, and cross-checking it
explainers.body: Not everything you read or watch is true or fair. Before you use a source, judge it. A reliable source lacks obvious bias, is kept up to date, is complete and free of errors, and comes from an author and publication you can check. Ask yourself four quick questions:
bullets: Who wrote or made it, and do they really know the topic? Can I find out who they are?
When was it made? Old information may be out of date.
Can I trust it? Does it give evidence, or only opinion? Is the argument convincing?
Is it relevant? Does it actually help answer my question, or is it merely interesting?

explainers.title: Skill 7 (1.2): Searching the internet well
explainers.body: Used well, a search engine saves time and finds better information. Used weakly, it means typing a whole sentence and clicking the first link. Strong searching follows clear steps:
bullets: Be clear about exactly what information you need before you start.
Choose three to six important keywords, not a full sentence.
Look past the first few results; strong sources are often further down.
Skim-read a page quickly. Is it clear, relevant and useful? If so, save or note it.
Check who made the page and when, using Skill 6, and plan to cross-check it.

explainers.title: Skill 8 (1.4): Reading a source closely and taking notes
explainers.body:
When you find a good source, you do not copy it. You read it closely and take notes in your own words. Stage 8 gives you a reliable method for getting to the heart of any text:

This method forces you to understand the source, not just recopy it, and it leaves you with tidy notes you can actually use. Writing in your own words also proves you understood the idea and keeps you clear of copying.
bullets: Give the whole text a title that captures its main idea. To find it, look for words that are repeated, because writers repeat what matters most.
Pick out the topic-specific words: the special words tied to the subject, such as emissions, congestion or filter for a traffic topic. Write them down; you will need them.
Give each paragraph a sub-heading that names its key idea.
Summarise each paragraph in your own words, in about two sentences.

explainers.title: Skill 9 (1.4): Summarising and synthesising from several sources
explainers.body:
A summary is a short version of a text, in your own words, that keeps only the most important ideas. But at Stage 8 you go one step further: you synthesise. To synthesise is to pull together what several sources say and combine it into your own findings, noticing where they agree and where they differ.

These sentence starters help you summarise a single source:

And these help you synthesise across sources, which is the real Stage 8 goal:
bullets: The text is about ...
The main idea is ...
In the first part, we learn ...
Later, it explains ...
Finally, it argues that ...
Both my sources agree that ...
However, one source claims ..., while the other says ...
Putting my sources together, I now think ...

explainers.title: Skill 10 (1.4): Recording and presenting your findings
explainers.body: Findings are only useful if others can understand them. After you gather information, especially from a questionnaire, record and organise it so a pattern shows, then present it in the clearest form for your audience and your purpose. Tables, tally charts and simple bar charts organise numbers; careful quotations bring interviews to life.

explainers.title: Skill 11 (1.2): Referencing accurately and building a reference list
explainers.body:
When you use someone else's work, you must give them credit by writing a reference. A reference says exactly where your information came from. A reference list gathers all your references together at the end of your work. In Stage 8 you are expected to reference accurately, and to reference even the sources you used to write your questionnaire.

Referencing matters for two reasons. First, it is honest: taking someone's words or ideas and passing them off as your own is called plagiarism, and we never do it. Second, it is useful: a reader can check your sources and trust your work more.

explainers.title: Staying safe and fair when you research
explainers.body:
Because research takes you out into the world and online, a good researcher also learns to stay safe and to be fair. These habits are part of the skill, not extra rules.

Staying safe online. When you search and read online, protect yourself:

Being fair to different perspectives. Global Perspectives is about seeing an issue from many sides. On almost any issue, thoughtful people hold different views, and a fair researcher listens to all of them evenly before deciding. Look at an issue from four levels: how it affects you personally, your local community, your nation, and the wider global world. Traffic and clean air look different at each level, and seeing all four makes your research much richer.
bullets: Never share your full name, home address, school details or photos with strangers online.
If a page asks you to sign up, download something, or 'click to win', stop and check with a trusted adult.
If a source upsets or worries you, close it and talk to your teacher or family.

explainers.title: How research feeds the other five skills
explainers.body:
Research is the first Global Perspectives skill for a reason: it feeds all the others. Once you have researched an issue well, the rest becomes possible.

So the effort you put into research now is never wasted. It is the foundation the whole subject is built on.
bullets: Analysis needs good information before you can break an issue into causes, effects and connections.
Evaluation needs trustworthy, cross-checked sources before you can judge how strong an argument is.
Reflection grows every time you notice how your research changed your mind.
Collaboration works better when everyone brings well-researched ideas and evidence to share.
Communication is only as strong as the research behind it; cross-checked facts make your message believable.

explainers.title: Putting it all together: the research cycle
explainers.body: You have now met every research skill in this unit. Here is how they fit into one cycle you can use for any issue:
bullets: Ask a clear, focused, arguable question, and break it into sub-questions.
Predict what you expect, and choose methods to test it.
Gather information from a range of primary and secondary sources.
Judge each source, and cross-check it against the others.
Read closely and take notes in your own words.
Synthesise your sources into your own findings.
Present your findings clearly, and reference every source.

explainers.title: What comes next
explainers.body: The next unit is Analysis. Once you can research an issue well, analysis teaches you to take it apart: to trace causes and effects, weigh consequences, and see how the pieces connect. Strong, cross-checked research now will make strong analysis much easier later. Well done for building your Stage 8 journey on a solid foundation.

bigIdeas.title: One big idea to hold on to
lines: In Global Perspectives, the topic is the vehicle and the skill is the destination.
We will travel through real issues such as traffic and clean air, growing towns, and work for young people.
But the aim is not to become an expert on traffic. The aim is to become a researcher who could find out about almost anything, fairly and well.

bigIdeas.title: A fairness note for Global Perspectives
lines: A strong researcher weighs many perspectives fairly, instead of pushing only their own.
Take a question such as: How could our school calendar respect the important days of every family it serves?
Answering it well means listening evenly to a family who observe Eid and a family who observe Christmas, and to families who mark neither, without favouring one.
Seeing an issue fairly from many sides, and only then forming your own view, is the very heart of Global Perspectives.

bigIdeas.title: Quick clues from a website address
lines: An address ending in .gov, often with a country code such as .gov.uk, is usually an official government site and is often reliable.
An address ending in .org is often a non-profit organisation. These can be good sources, but they may still lean towards a cause, so read with care.
If the address contains the word wiki, or the page is social media, be careful: anyone can edit it, so always cross-check it elsewhere.
Clues are not proof. Always check who wrote it and whether other good sources agree.

The most important Stage 8 habit is cross-checking, also called cross-referencing. Never rely on a single source. When two or three independent, trustworthy sources agree, you can be far more confident. When they disagree, that is a signal to dig deeper and find out why. Cross-checking is how you catch mistakes and bias before they get into your findings.

bigIdeas.title: What makes a good note
lines: Keep it short: a few words or one line, not a full paragraph.
Use bullet points and your own words, never copied word for word.
Write the source beside each note, so you can reference it later.
Note whether the point agrees or disagrees with your other sources, ready for cross-checking.

bigIdeas.title: The five parts of a reference
lines: 1. The author, or who wrote it.
2. The title, or what it is called.
3. The date it was published.
4. Where to find it, such as the website address.
5. The date you looked at it.

bigIdeas.title: Watch out for bias
lines: Bias is when a source leans unfairly to one side instead of being balanced.
A source is not automatically wrong because it has a viewpoint, but you should notice the viewpoint and weigh it.
Balance a strong opinion from one side by finding a good source from another side, and cross-check the facts.
Being fair does not mean having no opinion. It means forming your opinion only after hearing many sides.

bigIdeas.title: Quick clues from a web address
lines: Ends in .gov, often with a country code: usually an official government site, often reliable.
Ends in .org: often a non-profit organisation, usually useful, but it may lean towards a cause.
Contains wiki, or is social media: anyone may have edited it, so cross-check it elsewhere.
Clues are not proof. Always check who wrote it and whether other good sources agree.

bigIdeas.title: Cross-checking in three steps
lines: Find a second, independent source on the same fact.
If they agree, check that both sources are independent and trustworthy before using the fact with confidence.
If they disagree, dig deeper to find out why before you rely on either.

bigIdeas.title: Reference format and example
lines: Format: Author (Year). Title. [Online] Available at: web address (Accessed date).
Example: Diallo (2024). Traffic and Air Quality in Growing Cities. [Online] Available at: www.example.org/traffic-air (Accessed 14/05/2025).
This shows the format only; it is not a real source.
Sentence starters you can use when you write about a source:

bigIdeas.title: Your Challenge runs through everything
lines: Pick one global issue that also matters where you live. This is your Challenge.
You will build on it in every activity, so choose something you genuinely care about and can view from more than one side.
By the end you will have real, cross-checked research you can share with your teacher.

bigIdeas.title: A hint before you check with your tutor
lines: One is so broad you could study it for years and never finish.
One is a simple fact you could answer in one minute by counting.
One hides an opinion and pushes you to a single answer.
One can genuinely be argued, with evidence and different perspectives on both sides.

bigIdeas.title: The jumbled details
lines: Title: Cleaner Air for Growing Towns
Date you looked at it: 09/05/2025
Author: Costa
Web address: www.example.org/cleaner-air
Year published: 2023
Use this pattern: Author (Year). Title. [Online] Available at: web address (Accessed date). Write out your finished reference, then write a reference for one real source you found in Activity 6.

bigIdeas.title: Source passage: Traffic and the air we breathe
lines: As towns across the Horn of Africa grow, the number of cars, minibuses and taxis on the roads rises quickly. Busy junctions can fill with exhaust fumes, especially in the morning rush.

These fumes contain tiny particles that are harmful to breathe. Children, older people and anyone with a weak chest are affected most, and doctors link heavy traffic to more coughing and breathing problems.
Some towns have tried planting trees, improving buses so fewer people drive, and keeping the busiest streets clear of cars at peak times. Each idea has costs as well as benefits.

bigIdeas.title: What makes a good questionnaire question
lines: It uses words with clear meanings.
It is short and can be answered quickly.
It does not offer too many options.
It is not leading and contains no bias. A biased question pushes people toward one answer, such as: Don't you agree our air is terrible?
Check each question against that list. Rewrite any that is unclear, biased or leading. For example, change 'Don't you agree the air is bad?' into 'How would you describe the air near the junction?'

models.title: Research is part of everyday life too
lines: Imagine your family wants to choose a minibus route to school that is safe and good value.
You ask a clear question: which route is quickest, safest and cheapest in the morning rush?
You gather information from several sources: you time two routes yourself, ask three neighbours who travel daily, and check the fares.
You cross-check: one neighbour loves a route, but two others warn it floods when it rains, so you weigh that.
You bring it together and decide. That is real research, and you already do it without noticing.

So research is not a strange, school-only activity. It is a careful, honest way of finding things out that you can keep getting better at. This unit simply teaches you to do it on purpose, with more skill, about issues that matter to your community.

models.title: Sana's example: sharpening her question
lines: Sana's first attempt was: Why is traffic bad? That is vague, and it hides an opinion before she has any evidence.
Her second attempt was: What is air pollution? That is far too broad to finish.
Her strong final question is: How is the growth of traffic affecting the air we breathe in my neighbourhood, and what would help the most?
It is interesting, clear and focused on her neighbourhood, and it can be argued, because different people would suggest different solutions.

models.title: Sana's example: her sub-questions
lines: Big question: How is the growth of traffic affecting the air we breathe in my neighbourhood, and what would help the most?
Sub-question 1: How much has the traffic near my home grown in the last few years?
Sub-question 2: What does the traffic do to the air, and who is affected most?
Sub-question 3: How do different people, such as drivers, walkers and shopkeepers, see the problem?
Sub-question 4: What changes could reduce the pollution, and would people accept them?

Notice that each sub-question could be researched on its own. Sub-question 1 might need a traffic count she does herself; sub-question 2 might need a report from a health organisation; sub-question 3 calls for interviews with different people. Sub-questions turn one huge task into a set of doable ones, and they make sure you hear more than one perspective.

models.title: Tariq's example: sub-questions for a growing town
lines: Big question: As my town grows, what is happening to the open spaces where children play and birds nest?
Sub-question 1: Which open spaces have been built on in recent years?
Sub-question 2: What did people use those spaces for, and what have they lost?
Sub-question 3: What are the benefits of the new buildings, and who gains from them?
Sub-question 4: How could the town grow while keeping some green space?

A good set of sub-questions covers the issue from several angles: what is happening now, why it matters, who sees it differently, and what could change. If all your sub-questions ask almost the same thing, spread them out so they cover more of the issue and more viewpoints.

models.title: Zara's example: public transport in Hargeisa
lines: Zara wants to know why some people avoid the minibuses in Hargeisa.
Secondary sources: a news article about transport, and a transport charity's web page.
Primary sources: counting how full the buses are at a stop for an hour, and interviewing two regular passengers and one driver.
Together they give Zara a far fuller answer, and more than one perspective, than either type could alone.

Sources are also print or multimedia. Print sources are on paper: books, newspapers and printed reports. Multimedia sources are digital: websites, videos, audio and images. Each has strengths. A printed report may be checked carefully before it is published; a short video may explain an idea quickly. A Stage 8 researcher is comfortable with both, and never relies on only one kind.

models.title: Layla's example: work for young people
lines: Layla wants to know why some young people in her area struggle to find work after school.
Secondary sources: a report from a jobs charity, and a printed newspaper article about training courses.
Primary source: a respectful interview with an older cousin who searched for work for a year.
The report gives the big picture; the interview gives a real story, and a perspective, that no report could capture.

models.title: Sana's example: making and testing a prediction
lines: Sana's prediction: I think most families near the junction believe the air has become worse as the traffic has grown.
Best method: a short questionnaire given to many neighbours, because she wants numbers from a lot of people.
To go deeper, she also plans two interviews, one with a shopkeeper by the junction and one with a minibus driver, to hear two different perspectives.

models.title: Rami's example: matching method to question
lines: Rami predicts that solar lamps help students study after dark.
He chooses interviews with three families who already own solar lamps, because he wants their detailed experience, not just a yes or no.
He also plans one observation: visiting a home at night to see how the light is actually used.

The strongest research usually combines methods. A questionnaire tells you that many families think the air is worse; an interview tells you how that feels and why it matters; an observation shows you the traffic for yourself. Numbers, stories and observations together are far more convincing than any one alone.
Whatever method you choose, plan it kindly and safely. Ask people politely, let them say no, and never share anyone's name without permission. Good researchers respect the people who help them.

models.title: Sana's example: from a weak question to a strong one
lines: Weak, leading question: Don't you agree the traffic has ruined our air?
Strong, fair question: How would you describe the air quality near the junction compared with a few years ago?
Weak, too many options: it listed nine possible causes of pollution to tick.
Strong version: it offers three or four clear options, plus a space for other.

Once your questionnaire is written, test it. Give it to about ten people, collect their answers, and see which questions confused them or produced useless replies. Rewrite anything that did not work. Field-testing like this is exactly what Stage 8 research expects, and it is how professionals build good surveys.

models.title: Sana's example: cross-checking two sources
lines: Sana finds a health organisation's page saying traffic fumes can harm children's lungs, written by named experts and updated last year.
She finds a second page, an unsigned post with no date, claiming the fumes are harmless.
She trusts the first far more, then looks for a third reliable source to confirm it before she uses the fact.
Because two independent, trustworthy sources agree, she can now rely on the point in her findings.

models.title: Zara's example: searching about public transport
lines: Zara's question is about why people avoid the minibuses in her town.
Weak search: Why do people not want to take the minibus and what could make it better.
Strong keywords: public transport barriers safety cost.
She then looks for a transport organisation's report rather than the very first result, and notes it in her log to cross-check.

Choosing sharp keywords is a skill in itself. Pull out the two or three most important ideas in your question, search for those, then add or swap one word at a time until the results fit. Too many results? Add a word to narrow it. Too few? Remove a word or try a simpler one.

models.title: Sana's example: reading a report closely
lines: Sana reads a short report whose repeated words are traffic, fumes and children.
Her title for it: How traffic fumes affect children's health.
Topic-specific words she lists: emissions, congestion, asthma, particles.
Her sub-heading for paragraph two: who is most at risk. Her two-sentence summary, in her own words, captures the point without copying a single line.

models.title: Sana's example: synthesising her findings
lines: From her questionnaire: most neighbours believe the air has grown worse as the traffic has increased.
From a health report: traffic fumes are known to harm children's lungs.
From her interviews: a shopkeeper agrees the air is worse, while a driver feels the problem is exaggerated.
Her synthesis, in her own words: the evidence largely agrees the air has worsened with the traffic, though not everyone experiences it the same way.

When you summarise or synthesise, check three things: Is it the right length? Does it keep the key information? Is it in my own words, not copied? A good synthesis is short, fair to each source, and clearly your own thinking.

models.title: Sana's example: presenting her survey
lines: Sana asked 20 neighbours whether they thought the air near the junction had grown worse.
She sorted the answers into three groups: worse, about the same, and better.
A simple bar chart showed that 15 of the 20 said worse, which supported her prediction at a glance.
Alongside the chart she placed one short quotation from her shopkeeper interview, so readers hear a real voice too.

How you present depends on your audience and your information. Numbers usually suit a chart; personal stories usually suit a few quotations. Give every table and chart a clear heading and title so a reader understands it without help. Always choose the form that makes your finding easiest to grasp.

models.title: What a finished reference looks like
lines: Diallo (2024). Traffic and Air Quality in Growing Cities. [Online] Available at: www.example.org/traffic-air (Accessed 14/05/2025).
This shows the format only. Notice all five parts are present and in order.
You will practise real referencing in the Activities file and find ready-made starters in the Skills Toolkit.

models.title: Sana's whole journey, from worry to findings
lines: Skills 1 and 2: she turned a worry about traffic into an arguable question and four sub-questions.
Skills 3 and 4: she chose secondary reports and primary methods, and made a prediction to test.
Skill 5: she designed a questionnaire and tested it on her neighbours.
Skills 6 and 7: she searched well, judged her sources, and cross-checked her key fact.
Skills 8 and 9: she read closely, took notes in her own words, and synthesised her sources.
Skills 10 and 11: she presented her findings in a chart with a quotation, and referenced every source.

By following this cycle, Sana turned an everyday worry about the air into real, organised findings she can share with her teacher and her community. In the Activities file you will run the same cycle on your own Challenge, one step at a time, with your AI tutor beside you the whole way.

models.title: A model mind map: clean air and traffic
lines: In the middle: traffic and air in my neighbourhood.
Branches: How much has the traffic grown? What does it do to the air? Who is affected most? What do drivers think? What do walkers think? Would fewer cars help? Would more trees help?
Notice that these questions come from several angles and several perspectives, which is exactly what you want.

models.title: A model, in case you get stuck
lines: Issue: clean air and traffic in my neighbourhood.
Research question: How is the growth of traffic affecting the air we breathe, and what would help the most?
Sub-questions: How much has the traffic grown? What does it do to the air, and to whom? How do drivers and walkers see it? What changes would people accept?

models.title: Copying versus your own words
lines: Take the line: these fumes contain tiny particles that are harmful to breathe.
A copied note just repeats those exact words, which is not allowed.
A note in your own words might be: the exhaust holds small particles that are unhealthy to breathe in.
Same meaning, your words, shorter. That is the goal.

models.title: A model: Sana presenting her survey
lines: Cross-check: her questionnaire and a health report both suggest the air has worsened, so she is confident.
Finding: 15 of the 20 people she asked said the air near the junction is worse than before.
Best form: a simple bar chart, because the information is numbers and a chart shows the pattern instantly.
Audience: her teacher and community, who can see the problem at a glance, with one quotation added for a human voice.

toolkit.title: The research cycle at a glance
toolkit.intro: Whatever your issue, strong Stage 8 research follows the same seven steps. Come back to this list whenever you feel lost.
items: Question: ask a clear, focused, arguable question, and break it into sub-questions.
Predict and plan: say what you expect, and choose methods to test it.
Gather: collect information from a range of primary and secondary sources.
Check: judge each source, and cross-check it against the others.
Record: read closely and take notes in your own words.
Synthesise: bring your sources together into your own findings.
Present and reference: show your findings clearly, and say where every source came from.

toolkit.title: The Research skill, in plain words
toolkit.intro:
Research is finding out about something in a careful, organised way, from several sources, so that you can trust what you learn, weigh different perspectives, and explain it to someone else. It is not just typing a question into a search engine. Real research means asking a focused question that can be debated, gathering information from a range of sources, judging and cross-checking them, recording the important parts in your own words, synthesising them into your own findings, and saying where everything came from.

Three habits sit at its heart. Always use more than one source, because one source can be wrong or one-sided. Always cross-check important facts, because agreement between independent sources is what makes you confident. And always write in your own words and reference where your information came from, because that is honest and it helps others trust your work.

toolkit.title: Cambridge Stage 8 Research objectives
toolkit.intro: Global Perspectives sets out exactly what strong research looks like at this stage. Here are the official Stage 8 Research objectives, restated simply. Your teacher may refer to these codes.

rows: Construct relevant research questions.
Ask clear, focused questions that can be argued, and break them into sub-questions.
Identify and begin to reference a range of print and multimedia sources, and use them to locate relevant information and answer research questions.
Find and cross-check useful print and digital sources, use them to answer your question, and reference them accurately.
Select an appropriate method and conduct research to test predictions and begin to answer a research question.
Make a prediction, then choose and use the right method, such as a questionnaire, interview or observation, to test it.
Select, organise and record relevant information from a range of sources and findings from research, using appropriate methods.
Pick out what matters, take notes in your own words, synthesise your sources, and present your findings clearly.

toolkit.title: Primary and secondary sources
toolkit.intro: Strong research uses both types. Secondary sources give the bigger picture and facts others have found; primary sources tell you what is true in your own community, which no book could know. A good rule is to start with secondary sources to understand the issue, then use primary research to test it where you live, and cross-check the two against each other.

rows: Primary source
First-hand information you gather yourself.
An interview, a questionnaire you run, your own observation.
Secondary source
Information made earlier by someone else.
A book, a news article, a website, a report.

toolkit.title: Choosing a research method
toolkit.intro: Pick the method that fits what you want to find out. Make a prediction first, then use the method to test it. Combining two methods is often strongest.

rows: Questionnaire or survey
When you want numbers or opinions from many people.
How do people rate the air near the junction?
Interview
When you want one person's detailed views and perspective.
What is it like to drive a minibus through the rush?
Observation
When you want to know what really happens.
How many cars pass the school gate in ten minutes?
Secondary research
When you want the wider picture others have already found.
What do reports say about traffic and health?

toolkit.title: Turning a question into search keywords
toolkit.intro:
Search engines work best with a few sharp keywords, not a whole sentence. To make keywords, keep only the most important words in your question.

Then improve your search one step at a time: add a place, swap a word for a similar one, or make it more specific until the results fit. Too many results? Add a word. Too few? Remove one or try a simpler word.
items: Question: How is the growth of traffic affecting the air in my neighbourhood?
Weak search: type the whole question as a sentence.
Strong keywords: traffic air pollution health.

toolkit.title: Template: Reading a source and synthesising
toolkit.intro: Copy this table for each source. Keep notes short, in bullet points, and in your own words. The last row is where Stage 8 research really counts.

rows: Source and reference
Title I would give the text
Topic-specific words
Paragraph 1 sub-heading and note
Paragraph 2 sub-heading and note
Paragraph 3 sub-heading and note
Does it agree or disagree with my other sources?

toolkit.title: Sentence starters for summarising and synthesising
toolkit.intro:
Use these to summarise one source in your own words:

Use these to synthesise across several sources:

Then check: Is it the right length? Does it keep the key information? Is it fair to each source and in my own words?
items: The text is about ...
The main idea is ...
In the first part, we learn ...
Later, it explains ...
Finally, it argues that ...
Both my sources agree that ...
However, one source claims ..., while the other says ...
Putting my sources together, I now think ...

toolkit.title: Referencing your sources
toolkit.intro: A reference has five parts: the author, the title, the date published, where to find it, and the date you looked at it. Put all your references together in a reference list at the end of your work, and remember to reference even the sources you used to write your questionnaire. The easiest way to reference well is to write the source down the moment you use it.
items: According to ... (author, year), ...
One source, ... (author, year), explains that ...
As reported by ... (author, year), ...
This information comes from ... (author, year).

toolkit.title: Question starters for questionnaires and interviews
toolkit.intro:
Use these to write clear, fair questions. Keep them short and never leading.

Avoid starters like 'Don't you agree that ...?' or 'Isn't it obvious that ...?'. These are leading and biased, and push people toward one answer.
items: How often do you ...?
How would you describe ...?
What do you think about ...?
How far / how long / how many ...?
What would help you most with ...?
Can you tell me about a time when ...? (good for interviews)

checklists.title: Checklist: Is this a good research question?
checklists.intro: Tick each one. If you cannot tick them all, reword your question. Then break your question into three or four sub-questions that cover the issue from more than one perspective.
items: Interesting — it matters to me and to other people.
Clear — someone else would understand exactly what I am asking.
Focused — it is not too broad, too narrow or too vague.
Arguable — people could answer it differently, so I must weigh evidence and perspectives.
Findable — I will actually be able to find information to answer it.

checklists.title: Checklist: Can I trust this source, and does it agree with others?
checklists.intro: Ask these four questions about every source, then cross-check it.
items: Who wrote or made it, and do they really know the topic?
When was it made? Could it be out of date?
Can I trust it? Does it give evidence, is the argument convincing, and is it free of obvious bias?
Is it relevant? Does it actually help answer my question?

checklists.title: Checklist: A good questionnaire question
checklists.intro: Design your questions, then test them on about ten people and improve them. Each question should:
items: Use words with clear meanings.
Be short and quick to answer.
Not offer too many options.
Not be leading or contain bias.
Give a balance of quick yes or no questions and questions that invite detail.

challenge.intro: Look back at the topic list in the Lesson file (clean air and traffic, growing towns, public transport, work for young people, plastic waste, renewable energy, healthy food, road safety, water and sanitation, migration). Choose one that matters in your area, or think of your own. The best Stage 8 Challenge is one where thoughtful people disagree, because that gives you something to research and argue.
topics: Write your chosen issue in one sentence: 'The issue I am researching is ...'.
Write one reason you care about it.
Write one reason someone else in your community might see it differently from you.
checkpoints: I was surprised to discover that ...

activities.title: Mind-map your questions
activities.label: Activity 2: Mind-map your questions
activities.intro:
Before you pick a research question, you need lots of questions to choose from. A mind map gets them out of your head and onto the page.

Aim for quantity first. A messy map with many questions beats a tidy one with only two.
steps: Write your issue in the middle of a page and circle it.
Around it, write as many questions as you can, at least ten. Do not judge them yet; just get them down.
Draw lines linking questions that belong together, and mark any that look at the issue from a different perspective.

boxes.title: A model mind map: clean air and traffic
lines: In the middle: traffic and air in my neighbourhood.
Branches: How much has the traffic grown? What does it do to the air? Who is affected most? What do drivers think? What do walkers think? Would fewer cars help? Would more trees help?
Notice that these questions come from several angles and several perspectives, which is exactly what you want.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your mind-map questions to your AI tutor.
Ask it: which three questions look the most promising, and which capture more than one perspective?
Ask the tutor to suggest one strong question I did not think of.

activities.title: Rank weak and strong research questions
activities.label: Activity 3: Rank weak and strong research questions
activities.intro: Remember the four features of a good Stage 8 question: interesting, clear, focused, and able to be argued. Use them to judge the questions below. Rank these four from strongest (1) to weakest (4), and write a short reason for your order.
steps: A. What is air pollution?
B. How many cars pass my school gate in one minute?
C. Should our town limit cars in the busiest streets at peak times?
D. Why are cars bad?

boxes.title: A hint before you check with your tutor
lines: One is so broad you could study it for years and never finish.
One is a simple fact you could answer in one minute by counting.
One hides an opinion and pushes you to a single answer.
One can genuinely be argued, with evidence and different perspectives on both sides.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your ranking, strongest to weakest, with your reasons.
Ask whether it agrees, and to explain any place it would rank differently.
Ask the tutor to help me reword the weakest question until it can be argued.

activities.title: Write your research question and sub-questions
activities.label: Activity 4: Write your research question and sub-questions
activities.intro: Now build the research question for your Challenge. This question guides everything else, so take your time. It is completely normal to write it, decide it is weak, and rewrite it two or three times. That reworking is the skill, not a mistake.
steps: Write down what most interests you about your issue.
Draft three possible questions.
Choose or combine them into one research question that captures what you most want to find out.
Check it: is it interesting, clear, focused and arguable? Reword until all four are true.
Write four sub-questions that, answered together, would answer your main question, and that include more than one perspective.

boxes.title: A model, in case you get stuck
lines: Issue: clean air and traffic in my neighbourhood.
Research question: How is the growth of traffic affecting the air we breathe, and what would help the most?
Sub-questions: How much has the traffic grown? What does it do to the air, and to whom? How do drivers and walkers see it? What changes would people accept?

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Give your AI tutor your research question and four sub-questions.
Ask: is my question interesting, clear, focused and arguable? Where is it weakest?
Ask the tutor whether my sub-questions cover more than one perspective and really add up to my main question.

boxes.title: Bring it to your teacher
lines: Save your final research question and sub-questions.
Share them in your next teacher session and ask whether they suit the issue and can be argued.

activities.title: Sort the sources
activities.label: Activity 5: Sort the sources
activities.intro:
Warm up by sorting these. For each one, decide whether it is a primary source (first-hand, gathered by you) or a secondary source (made earlier by someone else). Then decide whether it is print or multimedia.

Write P or S, and print or multimedia, next to each letter. Then write one sentence, in your own words, explaining why strong research needs both primary and secondary sources.
steps: A. A questionnaire you give to twenty neighbours.
B. A news video about traffic in Mogadishu.
C. Counting cars at a junction for an hour and noting the number.
D. A printed government report on air quality.
E. An interview you record with a minibus driver.
F. A charity's web page about clean air.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your answers to your AI tutor and ask it to check them.
Ask it to explain any you got wrong, simply.
Ask the tutor: for my Challenge, would primary or secondary sources be more useful first, and why?

activities.title: Source hunt and referencing table
activities.label: Activity 6: Source hunt and referencing table
activities.intro:
Now find real sources for your question. Aim for a mix: at least one primary idea (a person you could interview, or something you could observe) and two secondary sources, including one print and one multimedia. Record each in a table like the one below, so your final reference list is easy later.

Use the four trust questions as you choose: Who wrote it? When? Can I trust it? Is it relevant? Reject any source you cannot trust, even if it is easy to find. Aim for quality: three sources you can cross-check are worth more than ten you cannot.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your table to your AI tutor.
Ask it: which of my sources looks the most reliable, and which the weakest, and why?
Ask the tutor to help me turn one row into a full, accurate reference with all five parts.

activities.title: Practise writing a reference
activities.label: Activity 7: Practise writing a reference
activities.intro: A reference has five parts: the author, the title, the date published, where to find it, and the date you looked at it. Below are the jumbled details of one source. Arrange them into a correct reference.

boxes.title: The jumbled details
lines: Title: Cleaner Air for Growing Towns
Date you looked at it: 09/05/2025
Author: Costa
Web address: www.example.org/cleaner-air
Year published: 2023
Use this pattern: Author (Year). Title. [Online] Available at: web address (Accessed date). Write out your finished reference, then write a reference for one real source you found in Activity 6.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your finished reference to your AI tutor and ask it to check all five parts are present and in order.
Ask it to help me reference one real source from my own source hunt.
Ask the tutor: why does the date I looked at a website matter?

activities.title: Close reading, notes and synthesis
activities.label: Activity 8: Close reading, notes and synthesis
activities.intro: Read the short passage below. It is one of your sources. You will give it a title, list its topic-specific words, take notes, then synthesise it with a second point.
steps: Give the whole passage a title that captures its main idea.
List three or four topic-specific words from the passage.
Give each paragraph a short sub-heading, then summarise each in two sentences in your own words.
Now synthesise: a second source (a neighbour) says the traffic does not bother them. Write one sentence combining the passage and the neighbour fairly, noting where they agree or differ.

boxes.title: Source passage: Traffic and the air we breathe
lines: As towns across the Horn of Africa grow, the number of cars, minibuses and taxis on the roads rises quickly. Busy junctions can fill with exhaust fumes, especially in the morning rush.

These fumes contain tiny particles that are harmful to breathe. Children, older people and anyone with a weak chest are affected most, and doctors link heavy traffic to more coughing and breathing problems.
Some towns have tried planting trees, improving buses so fewer people drive, and keeping the busiest streets clear of cars at peak times. Each idea has costs as well as benefits.

boxes.title: Copying versus your own words
lines: Take the line: these fumes contain tiny particles that are harmful to breathe.
A copied note just repeats those exact words, which is not allowed.
A note in your own words might be: the exhaust holds small particles that are unhealthy to breathe in.
Same meaning, your words, shorter. That is the goal.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your title, sub-headings and summaries to your AI tutor.
Ask it: have I copied any phrases, or is this genuinely in my own words?
Ask the tutor to check that my synthesis sentence is fair to both the passage and the neighbour.

activities.title: Design and test a questionnaire
activities.label: Activity 9: Design and test a questionnaire
activities.intro: Time for primary research: information you gather first-hand. First make a prediction, then design a questionnaire to test it, then test the questionnaire itself on real people.
steps: Write a prediction about your issue, starting with 'I think ...'.
Write five questions for your questionnaire. Include some quick yes or no questions and some that invite detail.
Decide who you will ask, and aim for about ten people.
After you collect the answers, note which questions confused people, and rewrite them.

boxes.title: What makes a good questionnaire question
lines: It uses words with clear meanings.
It is short and can be answered quickly.
It does not offer too many options.
It is not leading and contains no bias. A biased question pushes people toward one answer, such as: Don't you agree our air is terrible?
Check each question against that list. Rewrite any that is unclear, biased or leading. For example, change 'Don't you agree the air is bad?' into 'How would you describe the air near the junction?'

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your prediction and your five questions to your AI tutor. This is your peer review.
Ask it: are any questions leading, biased or unclear? How would you fix them?
Ask the tutor whether my questionnaire really tests my prediction.

boxes.title: A real-world step
lines: With a trusted adult's help, give your questionnaire to about ten family members or neighbours.
Collect the answers and bring them to your next teacher session to compare with your prediction.

activities.title: Cross-check and present your findings
activities.label: Activity 10: Cross-check and present your findings
activities.intro: Findings are only useful if they are reliable and clear. First cross-check, then present.
steps: Take one important fact you found. Name a second, independent source you could use to check it.
Write one sentence saying whether your two sources agree, and how confident that makes you.
Write your main findings so far in short bullet points.
Choose the clearest way to present them: a table, a simple bar chart, a short paragraph, or a few quotations. Give it a heading and title.
Write one sentence explaining why that form suits your information and your audience, then draft it.

boxes.title: A model: Sana presenting her survey
lines: Cross-check: her questionnaire and a health report both suggest the air has worsened, so she is confident.
Finding: 15 of the 20 people she asked said the air near the junction is worse than before.
Best form: a simple bar chart, because the information is numbers and a chart shows the pattern instantly.
Audience: her teacher and community, who can see the problem at a glance, with one quotation added for a human voice.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your key fact and the source you used to cross-check it.
Ask: ‘Are my two sources truly independent, or might one be repeating the other?’
Ask the tutor to check whether your chosen way of presenting the findings is clear for your audience.

activities.title: Looking ahead
activities.label: Looking ahead
activities.intro:
Everything you have gathered here is the raw material for the rest of your Global Perspectives year. In the next unit, Analysis, you will take these findings apart to trace causes and effects and see how they connect. Keep your research log, your sources and your reference list safe, because you will reach for them again.

Before you move on, do one last thing. Read back over your whole Challenge and ask yourself which single source you trust the most, and why. Being able to say why one source stands above the others is a sign that your research skill has genuinely grown this unit.

boxes.title: Share your progress
lines: Bring your findings, your chart and your reference list to your next teacher session.
Tell your teacher which perspective on your issue surprised you the most, and why.
Ask them one question about your Challenge that you have not been able to answer yet.

practice.intro: Answer these in your notebook or out loud with your AI tutor. There are 15 questions. Do not worry if some are tricky; that is how you find out what to practise next. Give your own words rather than copying from the other files.
practice.prompt: In your own words, what does 'research' mean at Stage 8?
practice.answer: Research means finding out about something in an organised way, from several sources, so you can trust it, weigh different views, and explain it. (Any answer with this idea is correct.)

practice.prompt: A good research question is interesting, clear, focused, and can be ______.
practice.answer: Argued (it can be argued).

practice.prompt: True or false: 'Why are cars bad?' is a strong research question.
practice.answer: False. It is vague and hides an opinion, so it is a weak question.

practice.prompt: What do we call the smaller questions you break a big research question into?
practice.answer: Sub-questions.

practice.prompt: Which of these is a primary source? (a) a textbook (b) a website (c) an interview you carry out (d) an encyclopaedia.
practice.answer: (c) an interview you carry out.

practice.prompt: Which of these is a secondary source? (a) a questionnaire you run (b) a news report (c) counting cars yourself (d) interviewing a driver.
practice.answer: (b) a news report.

practice.prompt: Name two of the five parts a reference should include.
practice.answer: Any two of: author, title, date published, where to find it (web address), date you looked at it.

practice.prompt: A question that pushes someone toward a particular answer is called a ______ question.
practice.answer: A leading question.

practice.prompt: To find the main idea of a text, it helps to look for words that are ______.
practice.answer: Repeated.

practice.prompt: What word means checking a fact against a second, independent source?
practice.answer: Cross-checking (cross-referencing).

practice.prompt: A web address containing the word ______ can be edited by anyone, so you should cross-check it.
practice.answer: Wiki (a web address containing wiki, or social media, can be edited by anyone).

practice.prompt: You want numbers from many people about how they travel. Which method fits best: questionnaire, interview, or observation?
practice.answer: A questionnaire (you want numbers from many people).

practice.prompt: Copying someone's words or ideas and passing them off as your own is called ______.
practice.answer: Plagiarism.

practice.prompt: What does it mean to synthesise your sources?
practice.answer: To synthesise is to combine what several sources say into your own findings, noting where they agree and differ.

practice.prompt: Give one reason why cross-checking a source matters.
practice.answer: Any one of: it catches mistakes or bias; two independent sources that agree make you more confident; a single source could be wrong or one-sided.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.intro: Match each research word (1 to 6) to the correct meaning (A to F). Write the pairs, such as 1-C.
practice.prompt: Primary source
options: A. Combining what several sources say into your own findings.
B. First-hand information you gather yourself, such as a questionnaire.
C. A note that says exactly where your information came from.
D. Copying someone's words or ideas and pretending they are your own.
E. Checking a fact against a second, independent source.
F. A statement of what you think will happen, which your research then tests.
practice.answer: B — First-hand information you gather yourself, such as a questionnaire.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Cross-check
practice.answer: E — Checking a fact against a second, independent source.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Prediction
practice.answer: F — A statement of what you think will happen, which your research then tests.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Reference
practice.answer: C — A note that says exactly where your information came from.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Synthesise
practice.answer: A — Combining what several sources say into your own findings.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Plagiarism
practice.answer: D — Copying someone's words or ideas and pretending they are your own.

practice.intro: These short scenarios ask you to use what you have learned. Write a sentence or two for each.
practice.prompt: Zara wants to know what drivers actually do at a busy junction in Hargeisa. Which method should she choose, and why?
practice.answer: Observation. Zara wants to know what drivers actually do, so watching and recording is the best method.

practice.prompt: Sana finds two web pages about traffic fumes. One ends in .org, names its authors and is dated this year; the other is an undated post with no author. Which should she trust more, and why?
practice.answer: The .org page with named authors and a recent date is more trustworthy, because you can check who wrote it and when, and it is more likely to be accurate than an undated, unsigned post.

practice.prompt: Tariq reads a report that keeps repeating the words open space, building and wildlife. What is he being told is the main idea?
practice.answer: The main idea is about how a growing town affects open space and wildlife. Repeated words point to the main idea.

practice.prompt: Rami found a useful fact on one website but forgot to note where it came from. What two problems will he face later?
practice.answer: Rami cannot reference the fact, so he cannot prove where it came from and a reader could not check it. He should have noted the source in his research log straight away.

practice.prompt: Layla has a questionnaire result and a report that seem to disagree. What Stage 8 habit should she use before she trusts either?
practice.answer: Cross-checking. She should look for a third reliable source, and find out why her two sources disagree, before trusting either.

reflection.prompt: Working on my own, at my own pace ...
Working with my AI tutor, my discussion partner ...
Working with my teacher in live sessions ...
Asking a family member or neighbour ...
Recording my work in my research log as I went ...

vocabulary.meaning: Finding out about something in an organised way, from several sources.
The main question, one you can argue, that guides your whole project.
A smaller question that helps you answer your main research question.
The point of view someone has, shaped by who they are and where they live.
Anywhere your information comes from: a person, book, website or video.
First-hand information you gather yourself, such as an interview or questionnaire.
Information made earlier by someone else, such as a book or website.
Information on paper, such as a book, newspaper or printed report.
Information in digital form, such as a website, video, image or audio.
The way you gather information, such as a questionnaire, interview or observation.
A written set of questions given to many people to gather information.
The activity of gathering information from many people, often using a questionnaire.
A deeper conversation with one person or small group to understand their views.
Carefully watching and recording what actually happens.
A statement of what you think will happen, or what is causing something, which research tests.
A question that unfairly pushes someone toward one answer.
When a source or question leans unfairly to one side instead of being balanced.
Able to be trusted; a reliable source is likely to be accurate and fair.
Checking a fact against a second, independent source; also called cross-referencing.
The most important point of a paragraph or a whole text.
Special words linked to a topic, such as emissions for a traffic topic.
A short heading that names the key idea of a paragraph.
Short reminders of the important ideas, written in your own words.
A short version of a text, in your own words, keeping only the key ideas.
To combine what several sources say into your own findings.
Actually useful for answering your particular question.
A note saying exactly where a piece of information came from.
All your references gathered together at the end of your work.
Copying someone's words or ideas and pretending they are your own.
Facts or information that support an idea or an answer.
A notebook or file where you record your research, sources and cross-checks as you go.

mistakes: Asking a question that is too broad, too narrow, or too vague, or that cannot be argued.
Using only one source, or only sources that agree with you.
Trusting a website without checking who wrote it and when, or without cross-checking it.
Copying words instead of taking notes in your own words.
Writing a leading or biased questionnaire question.
Forgetting to note where a fact came from, so you cannot reference it later.
Collecting lots of information but never synthesising or presenting it clearly.

selfAssessment.statement: I can explain what research means at Stage 8, including using several sources.
I can write a research question that is interesting, clear, focused and can be argued.
I can break a research question into helpful sub-questions.
I can tell primary from secondary, and print from multimedia sources.
I can make a prediction and choose a method to test it.
I can design a fair questionnaire and improve it after testing.
I can judge a source's reliability and cross-check it against another.
I can take notes in my own words and synthesise several sources.
I can present findings clearly and reference every source accurately.
